evals.prompt: Define VRIO in 2-3 sentences. Include all four tests and the kind of strategic question it answers.
expected_elements: Defines VRIO as a resource-based strategy or competitive advantage framework
Names Valuable
Names Rare
Names costly to Imitate or inimitable
Names Organized or organization to capture value
Explains it evaluates resources or capabilities
Connects passing all four tests to sustained competitive advantage

evals.prompt: Explain the mental model of VRIO. Name the primitives and describe how the sequential tests determine the competitive implication.
expected_elements: Names a resource or capability as the unit of analysis
Explains the relevant competitive context
Describes value as the first test
Describes rarity as dependent on the resource being valuable
Describes imitation cost as dependent on value and rarity
Describes organization as the ability to capture value
Maps failed gates to disadvantage, parity, temporary advantage, under-exploited advantage, or sustained advantage

evals.prompt: Why does a VRIO skill exist for agents? Name the common failure modes it prevents.
expected_elements: Prevents ordinary strengths being mislabeled as moats
Forces precise resource or capability definition
Forces value evidence tied to opportunities, threats, cost, revenue, risk, speed, quality, or options
Forces rarity comparison against competitors
Forces imitation-cost mechanism
Forces organization-to-capture-value analysis
Prevents final strategy claims from a flattering checklist

evals.prompt: Distinguish VRIO from Porter's Five Forces, SWOT/TOWS, Seven Powers, BCG Matrix, Ansoff Matrix, Playing to Win, and Expected Value. Give a mechanism-level reason each neighbor is different.
expected_elements: Porter's Five Forces analyzes external industry profit-pressure structure
SWOT/TOWS inventories internal/external factors and crosses them into options
Seven Powers classifies durable power-source categories
BCG Matrix allocates among portfolio units by market growth and relative market share
Ansoff Matrix classifies product-market growth paths
Playing to Win integrates strategic choices into a cascade
Expected Value compares options by probability and value
VRIO tests internal resources and capabilities for sustained advantage

evals.prompt: Place VRIO among strategy methods. What inputs feed it, what outputs should it produce, and which methods can follow it?
expected_elements: Classifies VRIO as resource-based view or internal competitive advantage analysis
Names inputs such as resource inventory, capability inventory, competitor comparison, or value evidence
Names outputs such as competitive implication, organization gap, protection priority, development action, or evidence gaps
Explains that Five Forces, SWOT/TOWS, Seven Powers, Playing to Win, Expected Value, BCG, or Ansoff can feed or follow it
Does not classify VRIO as an external industry analysis or portfolio allocation matrix

evals.prompt: Give an analogy for VRIO that preserves the sequential resource-test mechanism. Then name a bad analogy and explain what it loses.
expected_elements: Uses an analogy involving gates, checkpoints, filters, or tests
Preserves the order of value, rarity, imitation cost, and organization
Explains that a failed early gate changes the implication
Rejects an analogy that treats VRIO as a list of strengths
Rejects an analogy that makes VRIO an external market attractiveness tool

evals.prompt: Novel scenario: A company claims four advantages. A generic CRM setup improves sales execution but every competitor has one. A proprietary dataset improves pricing and only two rivals have comparable depth, but it could be replicated within a year. A trusted supplier network lowers costs, is rare, and depends on ten years of relationships, but procurement incentives prevent teams from using it. A machine-learning workflow improves retention, is rare, hard to imitate because it combines data, routines, and tacit know-how, and the organization has teams, incentives, systems, and metrics to exploit it. Apply VRIO and state evidence needed.
expected_elements: Classifies the generic CRM as valuable but not rare, implying competitive parity
Classifies the proprietary dataset as valuable and rare but not costly enough to imitate, implying temporary advantage
Classifies the supplier network as valuable, rare, and costly to imitate but not organized, implying under-exploited advantage or organization gap
Classifies the machine-learning workflow as a sustained advantage candidate
Names needed evidence for value, rarity, imitation cost, organization, or competitor comparison
Does not call every positive resource a moat
